The Roman Empire, spanning over 12 centuries, was a vast and complex entity that evolved from a small city-state in central Italy to a dominant world power. Its history can be broadly divided into three phases: the Roman Kingdom (753 BC - 509 BC), the Roman Republic (509 BC - 27 BC), and the Roman Empire (27 BC - 476 AD). The Roman Kingdom was characterized by the rule of seven kings, who laid the foundation for the city's future growth and expansion. The Roman Republic, marked by a system of governance where power was held by the Senate and the Assemblies, saw the rise of Rome as a major power in the Mediterranean, with conquests and alliances that expanded its territories and influence. The Roman Empire, established by Augustus Caesar in 27 BC, would go on to become one of the most powerful and enduring empires in history, leaving a lasting legacy in law, architecture, governance, and culture.
